processing: Medium oxidation of very large, round leaves, strip-rolled and charcoal roasted to a medium level; the thick leaf stands a solid roast without losing its fruit.
harvest_season: One spring picking, late April to early May, as mature shoots with three or four big open leaves.
appearance_dry: Large, broad, loosely twisted dark strips, visibly bigger than Shui Xian, with a sweet baked-pear smell.
appearance_wet: Very large, round, thick olive leaves with red rims, among the largest wet leaves on the Wuyi table.
taste_profile: Baked pear and citron fruit with soft honey and a warm roast, a smooth medium body and a mild, cooling mineral finish.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, gaiwan or zisha pot. The big leaves take a moment to open, so the second steep is often better than the first; do not crowd the vessel or they will have nowhere to go.

vintage_note: Spring harvest of the current year, roasted over the summer and sold from autumn with the year stated. Medium-roasted Fo Shou drinks well on release and keeps two to four years sealed and dry; it is rarely aged on purpose but takes a re-roast well.
description:
Fo Shou, Buddha's hand, is a huge-leaved cultivar from southern Fujian that Wuyi makers have adopted for rock tea, where it goes by the local nickname Xue Li, snow pear, because the cup smells of ripe pear. It is one of the better-value yancha: not a famous bush, but a distinctive one.

The cultivar comes from Yongchun county in Minnan, where it has been grown for a long time and where a traditional story has it grafted onto a citron tree (fo shou is also the name of the fingered citron fruit); the story is a story, but the leaves really are enormous, round and soft, among the largest of any Fujian cultivar. In Yongchun it is made as a ball-rolled Minnan oolong; in Wuyi it is made as strip-rolled, charcoal-roasted yancha, and the two taste like different teas.

The Wuyi version is picked mature in spring, shaken through the night to a medium oxidation, rolled and roasted, usually to a medium level. The big leaf has enough substance to take that roast without going hollow, and the fruit survives it: baked pear, a citron-peel note, honey and a warm toastiness, on a smooth body with a modest mineral finish.

Brew it like any rock tea, boiling water and a full gaiwan, but give the leaves room; they open to a size that surprises people and the second and third steeps are the best. It lasts seven or eight infusions and is an easy tea for food or for drinkers who find Rou Gui too sharp.

It is sold by the current spring, mostly from plantings outside the core scenic area, which is why it is affordable; look for whole, long strips and a clean roast, and a stated year. For the same leaf in its home style, try Yongchun Fo Shou, which is greener, rounder and tastes of fresh rather than baked fruit.
sources_note: The Wikipedia article covers both the Yongchun and the Wuyi versions, hence exact scope. Xue Li as the Wuyi name for Fo Shou is the standard local usage; the citron-grafting origin is a legend and is flagged as such.
history:
Fo Shou is first of all a Yongchun plant: the tea is produced in that county in southern Fujian and is a national geographical indication product. It is also made in Wuyi and in Taiwan.

The Wuyi version is the same kind made as rock tea, and the local name Xue Li, snow pear, is said to refer to its pear-like character. When and by whom it reached Wuyi is little documented, and it is not among the old named bushes with long stories attached.
